title: Require independent public accuracy testing before any law-enforcement procurement of facial recognition
description: Illustrative reference decision modelled on the ACLU's 2018 test of Amazon Rekognition against members of Congress. Not a documented decision of any specific organization.

history.note: Initial Edition 1.1 content, part of the Phase 3 canonical expansion. Deliberately reuses the existing biometric-safeguards pattern, control, evidence type, and board question from Edition 1.0's Rite Aid/Clearview cluster (PAT-007, CTR-007, EVI-006, BRD-007) rather than creating near-duplicate objects — this incident is a variant of the same governance concept, applied at the procurement stage rather than post-deployment.

Normalized US/UK spelling variants to the American-English house style (schema field names, e.g. organizations_involved, are already American; majority framework citations - NIST, FTC, EEOC, FCRA, BIPA - are American sources).

decision_statement: Before any government body procures facial-recognition technology for law-enforcement use, an independent third party must test the vendor's system for demographic-disaggregated accuracy on a realistic dataset, with results published, and procurement must not proceed if the results are not independently reproducible or show significant disparity.
decision_context: Motivated by the ACLU's demonstration that Amazon Rekognition, at default settings, falsely matched 28 members of Congress to mugshots with people of colour disproportionately misidentified — a test conducted by a third party after the technology was already in use by law enforcement, rather than before procurement.
governing_body: Illustrative example — Law Enforcement Technology Procurement Board
alternatives_considered: Rely on the vendor's own accuracy claims without independent verification.
Test accuracy only after a procurement decision has already been made and the system deployed.

citations.title: Amazon's Face Recognition Falsely Matched 28 Members of Congress With Mugshots

relationships.reason: This decision is modelled as a direct governance response to this test.

This decision reuses the existing biometric safeguards pattern rather than defining a new one — demographic-disaggregated accuracy testing is already this pattern's core mechanism, and applying it pre-procurement rather than post-deployment doesn't change what the pattern does.
Law enforcement facial recognition is explicitly named among the high-risk categories this control's Annex III lists, making it a direct, not inflated, application.
The existing facial-recognition accuracy log evidence type already covers exactly this requirement.
The existing biometric consent-and-accuracy board question already covers this concern.
